The author's characteristic manner is the comic metaphysic carried in the deadpan of the civil servant.
historical_context: Dublin in the war years, and the Irish Times. The record dates the work as composed between 1940 and 1945 and first published in 1940 and it is catalogued under critical essay and the modern review; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
literary_significance: The Cruiskeen Lawn column is the finest comic journalism in Irish English: its glosses, its pseudonyms and its learned jokes made the daily column a literary form of the war years.
attribution_notes: It was published under the name Myles na gCopaleen, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to Flann O'Brien is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1940, as newspaper column (the irish times, as myles na gcopaleen), by Flann O'Brien. Composed between 1940 and 1945. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Ploughman and Other Poems
description: The first collection: the ploughman's lyric of the Monaghan field. It is a verse work of 1936 by Patrick Kavanagh; it is catalogued here under Georgian Anthology Lyric; Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: The Ploughman and Other Poems gathers Kavanagh's first lyrics of the Monaghan field, the ass, the fair and the plough, in the plain line of the ploughman's speech charged with the clay.
narrative_structure: A collection of Monaghan lyrics of the field and the fair. A collection of separate short poems in the anthology manner, ordered by subject rather than by narrative. A collection of poems written to be performed, each a separate monologue or song in the spoken dialect.
literary_form: Poetry collection (the Monaghan lyric)
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the Georgian lyric manner: the rhymed stanza of four or eight lines, the plain monosyllabic diction, the observed countryside and the elegiac undertone, without the modernist break in syntax. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the plain line of the ploughman's speech charged with the clay.
historical_context: Monaghan in the 1930s, and the Irish lyric of the small farm. The record dates the work as composed between 1933 and 1935 and first published in 1936 and it is catalogued under georgian anthology lyric; dialect poem and vernacular performance.
literary_significance: The Ploughman and Other Poems made Kavanagh the ploughman-poet of Ireland: its lyrics of the field and the ass are the plain voice of the small farm in the Irish lyric of the century.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Patrick Kavanagh. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1936, as poetry collection (the monaghan lyric), by Patrick Kavanagh. Composed between 1933 and 1935. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Green Fool
description: The autobiography of the country boy and the green fool of the title. It is a prose work of 1938 by Patrick Kavanagh; it is catalogued here under Autobiography and the Modern Memoir; Memoir and Autobiographical Prose and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: The Green Fool recounts the country boyhood of the Monaghan farm, the school, the fair and the first poems, in the prose of the country boy in the city that made Kavanagh's name.
narrative_structure: An autobiography in chapters of the boyhood and the farm. An autobiography in chapters, the formative scenes set piece by set piece, with letters and diaries quoted at the turning points. A memoir of a life or a period, the remembered scene and the quoted letter carrying the account.
principal_characters: the country boy; the farm; the school; the fair
literary_form: Autobiography (the country boyhood)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of autobiography: the first-person narrative of the life, the set-piece of the formative scene, the quotation from letters and diaries, and the reflection on the formation of a self. The author's characteristic manner is the plain line of the ploughman's speech charged with the clay.
historical_context: Monaghan in the 1910s and 1920s. The record dates the work as composed between 1936 and 1937 and first published in 1938 and it is catalogued under autobiography and the modern memoir; memoir and autobiographical prose.
literary_significance: The Green Fool is Kavanagh's autobiography of the country boyhood and the companion to the lyrics: its farm and its green fool made the small farm of Monaghan a subject of Irish autobiography.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Patrick Kavanagh. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1938, as autobiography (the country boyhood), by Patrick Kavanagh. Composed between 1936 and 1937. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Great Hunger
description: The long poem of the clay, the potato and the celibate farmer of Monaghan. It is a verse work of 1942 by Patrick Kavanagh; it is catalogued here under Modernist Long Poem and the Mythical Method; Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: The Great Hunger follows Patrick Maguire, the celibate farmer of the Monaghan clay, through the farming year, the potato and the hunger of the body and of the soul, in the long poem that answered the Ireland of the revival with the Ireland of the parish.
narrative_structure: A long poem in sections of the farming year and the hunger. A long poem built as a sequence of fragments in several voices, ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative sequence. A collection of poems written to be performed, each a separate monologue or song in the spoken dialect.
principal_characters: Patrick Maguire; the clay; the mother; the parish
literary_form: Long poem (the clay and the celibate farmer)
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the modernist long poem: the polyphonic sequence of fragments in free verse and in borrowed metres, quotation and allusion doing the work of connective argument, the whole ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative. The author's characteristic manner is the plain line of the ploughman's speech charged with the clay.
historical_context: Monaghan in the 1930s and 1940s, published in 1942. The record dates the work as composed between 1940 and 1941 and first published in 1942 and it is catalogued under modernist long poem and the mythical method; dialect poem and vernacular performance.
literary_significance: The Great Hunger is the greatest Irish poem of the twentieth century before the war's end: its Maguire, its clay and its celibacy made the parish the matter of the long poem and answered the Ireland of the revival with the Ireland of the field.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Patrick Kavanagh. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1942, as long poem (the clay and the celibate farmer), by Patrick Kavanagh. Composed between 1940 and 1941. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Grey Coast
description: The first novel of the Scottish Renaissance's northern coast. It is a prose fiction work of 1926 by Neil Gunn; it belongs to The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival and it is catalogued here under Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle.
plot_or_argument: The Grey Coast sets the young man of the Caithness coast against the fishing village, the sea and the southward pull of the modern world, and follows his quarrel with the north through the years before and after the war, in the charged plain prose that became the manner of Gunn's northern novels.
narrative_structure: A novel of the coast in chapters of the season and the return. A continuous prose narrative in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution.
principal_characters: the young man of the coast; the fishing village folk; the southward employer
literary_form: Novel (the Caithness coast); provincial novel
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction: the continuous chaptered narrative carries description, dialogue and reflection. The author's characteristic manner is the prose of the northern coast and the sea, charged but plain.
historical_context: Caithness and the north of Scotland in the years of the Scottish Renaissance. The record dates the work as composed between 1924 and 1925 and first published in 1926 and the corpus places it within The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival, it is catalogued under provincial novel and the british rural chronicle.
literary_significance: The Grey Coast is the founding novel of Gunn's north and one of the first novels of the Scottish Renaissance: its coast, its village and its quarrel made the Gaelic north a world of the modern Scottish novel.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Neil Miller Gunn. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1926, as novel (the caithness coast), by Neil Gunn. Composed between 1924 and 1925. The record grades the work as secondary canon.
